## From Categorical Nosology to Dynamical Systems Theory

Current psychiatric classification systems, such as the DSM, largely rely on categorical models that treat mental disorders as distinct entities. However, this framework often fails to capture the fluid reality of clinical practice, where patients frequently present with heterogeneous symptoms, extensive comorbidity, and diagnostic shifts over time [@Joober2019]. The limitations of viewing psychiatric conditions as static "essences" have prompted a shift toward Dynamical Systems Theory (DST), which conceptualizes psychopathology not as a fixed disease entity, but as a specific dynamical state of the brain and body [@Maj2005; @Kendler2015; @Joober2019].

In this view, the vast array of neurobiological and psychosocial variables that define a person's mental state can be mapped onto a high-dimensional state space. Within this space, the mental state evolves along specific trajectories governed by the system's underlying rules of evolution. Rather than exploring the entire state space, these trajectories tend to converge toward stable points known as attractors, while the surrounding regions that pull the system toward a specific attractor are called as basins of attraction. Psychiatric symptoms can be conceptualized as specific attractors within this landscape. While a healthy individual maintains the flexibility to transition between various attractors, a mental illness manifests when the system becomes trapped within deep, maladaptive basins that resist the transitions to other basins [@Salvi2021; @schefferEtAl2024a; @ngr2025].

## Neural Architecture as a Potential Energy Landscape

While the concept of state space and attractor landscape provides a plausible metaphor for clinical symptoms, precise physical grounding in the brain's functional organization remains a subject of ongoing investigation. It is increasingly hypothesized that the network structure of brain at variuos levels of organization shapes the geometry of the state space [@gu2018]. Within this framework, the matrix of synaptic weights ($W$) is thought to define a potential energy surface, or "landscape", where the altitudes represent levels of neural activation [@watanabe2014].

For example, recent research on connectome harmonics and the eigenmodes of cortical traveling waves suggests that multi-scale structural connectivity provides a natural set of basis functions for brain dynamics [@atasoy2016; @abdelnour2018; @haggarty2025]. Connectome harmonics—the eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian derived from the structural connectivity matrix—form the basis or dimensions of the attractor landscape, thereby constraining how neural systems evolve . Spontaneous and task-evoked activity patterns can be expressed as weighted superpositions of these intrinsic eigenmodes, visualized as specific coordinates within the state space. Consequently, structural connectivity (SC) does not merely support functional connectivity (FC); it defines the low-dimensional manifold within which neural trajectories unfold [@abdelnour2018].

The synaptic weight matrix (W) shapes the spectrum of the Laplacian, thereby determining which modes are energetically favorable, how easily transitions between modes occur, and how stable particular configurations become [@delange2014]. In this sense, it can be understood that alterations in SC or FC reshape the eigen-spectrum, which in turn deforms the geometry of the attractor landscape. Empirical studies using connectome spectral analysis in depression have shown that pathological states are associated with altered occupancy and energy distribution across harmonics, consistent with a reconfiguration of the underlying state space [@atasoy2017].

As the systems' state evolves according to dynamic rules, it behaves like a ball rolling across this landscape. Stable equilibrium points at the bottom of valleys represent attractors, while unstable peaks and ridges act as repellors that push the system toward neighboring basins. The "dynamic resilience" of any given state, as described by Scheffer et al.[@schefferEtAl2024a], is determined by the basin's depth and the steepness of its slopes. In a resilient healthy system, deep basins allow the brain to absorb significant perturbations and rapidly return to a stable equilibrium.

## Noise, Stability, and the Erosion of Resilience

Research on dynamic functional connectivity (DFC) has revealed that functional connectivity is in a state of constant flux. Furthermore, neural ensembles exhibit modular variability, shifting their activity across different functional modules depending on the context. This variability suggests that the attractor landscape, constrained by underlying connectivity, is continuously fluctuating. Such inherent flexibility ensures that attractor basins remain sufficiently malleable, allowing the system to absorb perturbations. This property provides the dynamic resilience necessary to maintain a healthy equilibrium [@Webb2011; @Rolls2012].

Psychopathology often emerges when certain changes in SC or FC alter and rigidify this attractor landscapes. This erosion of dynamic resilience makes the healthy basins fragile; as they become shallower and more rigid, even minor life stressors can push the systems' state over a repellor into a pathological basin [@schefferEtAl2024a].

## The Paradox of Persistence: Hysteresis and Network Rigidity

Hysteresis refers to the tendency for a system to remain trapped in a maladaptive state even after the initiating stressor has vanished. While healthy basins of attraction may be degraded and shallow, pathological states often develop intense local hyper-connectivity, resulting in deep, rigid basins [@SvozCouche2017]. This "trapping" is rooted in multi-scale deficits that span from synaptic architecture to large-scale network dynamics.

At the synaptic level, depression is closely associated with impaired neuroplasticity and structural erosion, including decreased dendritic spine density, impaired long-term potentiation (LTP), and reduced expression of plasticity-related molecules such as BDNF [@Price2010; @Duman2012; @Kang2012; @Duman2016]. These cellular-level deficits translate into macroscopic abnormalities in large-scale functional networks, particularly within the Default Mode Network (DMN) [@Yan2019; @Tozzi2021].

In healthy individuals, DFC exhibits significant flexibility, allowing the brain to transition seamlessly between a diverse repertoire of attractor states. In contrast, patients with depression exhibit reduced temporal variability and a restricted state repertoire. This network rigidity leads to excessive occupancy in sub-optimal states, most notably the depressive rumination associated with the hyper-segregated DMN [@Kaiser2016; @Demirta2016; @DOstilio2016; @Regonia2021; @Durstewitz2021; @An2024].

## Therapeutic Recovery as Landscape Reshaping

This model implies that recovery requires reshaping the attractor landscape. Because pathological basins can be very deep and rigid (hysteresis), small perturbations often fail to dislodge the system. Intensive treatments, such as ECT, rTMS, and psychedelics, may provide enough energy to reset the system, and then allowing the system to settle into a new set of attractors (see Figure \@ref(fig:health_ECT)).

For example, psychedelic의 효과를 설명하는 다양한 모델 중 하나인 "RElaxed Beliefs Under Psychedelics (REBUS)"[@CarhartHarris2019] integrates the "Entropic Brain" hypothesis with a predictive processing framework. The REBUS model postulates that psychedelics, through their $5\text{-HT}_{2\text{A}}$ agonism, induce a dysynchronization of higher-order cortical regions [@siegel2024]. This manifests as a relaxed precision-weighting on high-level prior beliefs, effectively decreasing the "stiffness" of the top-down cognitive constraints.

In a control-theoretic formulation, this acute perturbation was described as a "transient flattening of the control-energy landscape" [@Madsen2021; @Singleton2022]. Mechanistically, psychedelics lower the minimum energy required to transition between recurrent brain states, operationalized as a reduction in the energetic barriers separating diverse attractors. Greater energy-barrier reduction has been associated with shorter state dwell times and more entropic state sequences, consistent with a increase in attractor malleability and enhanced exploration of the brain's state space. Whether through the broad physiological "reset" of ECT or the desynchronization of psychedelics, the goal of these treatments remains consistent: to provide the system an opportunity to remodel the attractor landscape to healthy states [@Rao2018; @Rolls2020].
